Anatomy-05.question: ১) Length of esophagus-
Anatomy-05.exp:
The correct answer is 25 cm. The adult oesophagus is approximately 25 cm long, extending from the pharynx (C6 vertebral level) to the gastro-oesophageal junction (T11 level).

Important anatomical points:

  • Length: ~25 cm

  • Diameter: ~2 cm

  • Passes through the diaphragm at T10 level

  • Opens into stomach at T11 level

The other options are incorrect because:

  • 15 cm → Too short; approximate length of some segments only.

  • 35 cm → Longer than normal oesophagus.

  • 40 cm → Approximate length of the entire upper GI tract segment, not oesophagus.

High-yield points:

Oesophagus:

  • Length = 25 cm

  • Begins = C6

  • Diaphragm passage = T10

  • Gastro-oesophageal junction = T11

Exam pearl:
Adult oesophagus length = 25 cm.

Anatomy-05.question: ২) Renal angle is -
Anatomy-05.option1: Angle between 12th rib and edge of Transeverse abdominis muscle
Anatomy-05.option2: Angle between 12th rib and edge of Trapezeus muscle
Anatomy-05.option3: Angle between 12th rib and edge of erector spinae muscle
Anatomy-05.option4: Angle between 12th rib and edge of External oblique muscle
Anatomy-05.exp:
The correct answer is the angle between the 12th rib and the lateral border of the erector spinae muscle. This is known as the renal angle (costovertebral angle).

Clinical importance:

  • Located in the posterior flank

  • Corresponds to the location of the kidneys

  • Tenderness in this area suggests renal pathology, especially acute pyelonephritis

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Transverse abdominis muscle → Not the boundary of the renal angle.

  • Trapezius muscle → Upper back muscle, not related to renal angle.

  • External oblique muscle → Abdominal wall muscle, not a boundary of renal angle.

High-yield points:

Renal angle (CVA):

  • Formed by: 12th rib + lateral border of erector spinae muscle

  • Tenderness → Renal inflammation (e.g., pyelonephritis)

Exam pearl:
Renal angle = 12th rib + erector spinae muscle.

Anatomy-05.question: ৩) Most important factors which keep the Liver in position
Anatomy-05.exp:
The correct answer is coronary ligament. The coronary ligament is the most important peritoneal attachment that helps maintain the position of the liver.

The liver is held in position by:

  • Coronary ligament (main stabilizing attachment)

  • Falciform ligament

  • Triangular ligaments

  • Hepatic veins (help anchor the posterior surface)

The other options are less appropriate because:

  • Hepatic veins → Provide vascular attachment but are not the main ligamentous support.

  • Right triangular ligament → Helps attach the right lobe but is a smaller supporting structure.

  • Falciform ligament → Divides the liver into anatomical right and left lobes and provides support, but is not the primary stabilizer.

High-yield points:

Main supports of liver:

  • Coronary ligament = most important

  • Falciform ligament

  • Right and left triangular ligaments

  • Hepatic veins

Exam pearl:
Liver position is mainly maintained by the coronary ligament.

Anatomy-05.question: ৪) Ito cell present in-
Anatomy-05.exp:
The correct answer is Space of Disse. Ito cells (hepatic stellate cells) are located in the perisinusoidal space of Disse between:

  • Hepatocytes

  • Sinusoidal endothelial cells

Functions of Ito cells:

  • Store vitamin A

  • Produce extracellular matrix (collagen)

  • Become activated in liver injury → contribute to hepatic fibrosis and cirrhosis

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Space of Mall → A periportal space involved in lymphatic drainage, not the location of Ito cells.

  • In the vessel wall → Not the location of hepatic stellate cells.

  • None of above → Incorrect.

High-yield points:

Ito cells = Hepatic stellate cells

  • Location: Space of Disse

  • Function: Vitamin A storage

  • Activated in chronic liver injury → fibrosis

Exam pearl:
Ito cell → Space of Disse → Hepatic fibrosis.

Anatomy-05.question: ৫) Present in small intestine
৬) Most numerous mucous glands of prostate are contained within
৭) Motilin is secreted from which cell?
৮) Urethra passes through which part of penis?
৯) Ovarian artery is a branch of
Anatomy-05.exp:
The correct answer is abdominal aorta. The ovarian arteries are paired branches that arise directly from the abdominal aorta, usually just below the renal arteries.

Key points:

  • Supply: Ovary, uterine tube, and part of uterus

  • Course: Descend in the suspensory ligament of the ovary

  • Anastomose with the uterine artery (branch of internal iliac artery)

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Common iliac artery → Gives rise to internal and external iliac arteries, not ovarian arteries.

  • Internal iliac artery → Gives the uterine artery, which supplies the uterus and anastomoses with ovarian artery.

  • External iliac artery → Continues as femoral artery; not related to ovarian blood supply.

High-yield points:

Female pelvic arterial supply:

  • Ovarian artery → Abdominal aorta

  • Uterine artery → Internal iliac artery

Exam pearl:
Ovarian artery is a direct branch of the abdominal aorta.

Anatomy-05.question: ১০) Meckel's diverticulum is a remnant of:
Anatomy-05.exp:
The correct answer is Vitello-intestinal duct (omphalomesenteric duct). Meckel's diverticulum is a congenital remnant of the vitelline duct, which normally connects the embryonic midgut to the yolk sac and disappears during development.

Features of Meckel's diverticulum:

  • Located in ileum

  • True diverticulum (contains all layers of bowel wall)

  • May contain ectopic gastric or pancreatic tissue

  • Can cause bleeding, inflammation, or obstruction

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Müllerian duct → Gives rise to female reproductive tract (uterus, fallopian tubes, upper vagina).

  • Wolffian duct (mesonephric duct) → Gives rise to male reproductive tract structures.

  • Mesonephric duct → Same embryological origin as Wolffian duct; not related to Meckel's diverticulum.

High-yield points:

Meckel's diverticulum = Vitelline duct remnant

Rule of 2s:

  • 2 feet from ileocaecal valve

  • 2 inches long

  • 2% population

  • 2 types of ectopic tissue (gastric, pancreatic)

Exam pearl:
Meckel's diverticulum → Persistent vitello-intestinal (omphalomesenteric) duct.

Anatomy-05.question: ১১) The inferior vena cava is formed at right side of the body of -
Anatomy-05.exp:
The correct answer is vertebra L5. The inferior vena cava (IVC) is formed by the union of the right and left common iliac veins on the right side of the body of the fifth lumbar vertebra (L5).

Important anatomical points:

  • Formation: L5 vertebral level

  • Position: Right of the abdominal aorta

  • Passes through diaphragm: T8 level

  • Ends in right atrium

The other options are incorrect because:

  • T8 vertebra → Level where the IVC passes through the diaphragm, not where it is formed.

  • L6 vertebra → No L6 vertebra in normal human anatomy.

  • T10 vertebra → Level of oesophageal hiatus, not related to IVC formation.

High-yield points:

IVC anatomy:

  • Formed → L5

  • Diaphragm passage → T8

  • Opens into → Right atrium

Exam pearl:
IVC formation = Right & left common iliac veins at L5.

Anatomy-05.question: ১২) Dominant hormone in proliferative stage of menstrual cycle
১৩) Homologus structure of penis in female
১৪) The portal hepatic lobule emphasizes
Anatomy-05.exp:
The correct answer is exocrine function of hepatocyte. The portal lobule is designed to emphasize bile secretion, which is the exocrine function of hepatocytes.

  • Portal lobule is a triangular unit with:

    • Portal triad at the centre

    • Three surrounding central veins at the corners

  • It highlights the flow of bile from hepatocytes → bile ductules → portal triad

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Endocrine function of hepatocyte → Emphasized by the classical hepatic lobule, which focuses on blood flow and hepatocyte interaction with blood.

  • Oxygen content of blood → Related to blood supply gradients in the classical lobule/acinar model.

  • Nutrient content of blood → Mainly emphasized by the hepatic acinus model.

High-yield points:

Model Main function emphasized
Classical lobule Blood flow & metabolic function
Portal lobule Bile secretion (exocrine function)
Hepatic acinus Oxygen/nutrient gradients

Exam pearl:
Portal lobule → Exocrine function → Bile secretion.

Anatomy-05.question: ১৫) Accessory digestive organs exclude
১৬) Which of the following is the shortest part of male urethra?
Anatomy-05.exp:
The correct answer is membranous urethra. It is the shortest and least distensible part of the male urethra.

Length of parts of male urethra:

  • Prostatic urethra → ~3 cm (longest part)

  • Membranous urethra → ~1–2 cm (shortest part)

  • Penile (spongy) urethra → ~15 cm (longest segment)

  • Bulbar urethra → Part of spongy urethra

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Prostatic urethra → Longest and widest part; passes through prostate.

  • Bulbar urethra → A segment of spongy urethra, longer than membranous urethra.

  • Penile urethra → Long segment within corpus spongiosum.

High-yield points:

Male urethra:

  • Total length ≈ 18–22 cm

  • Shortest part = Membranous urethra

  • Longest part = Penile/spongy urethra

  • Most fixed part = Membranous urethra

Exam pearl:
Shortest male urethral segment = Membranous urethra.

Anatomy-05.question: ১৭) Gastric ulcer occurs typically along
Anatomy-05.exp:
The correct answer is lesser curvature. Gastric ulcers most commonly occur along the lesser curvature, particularly near the incisura angularis.

Reasons:

  • This area has relatively less mucosal protection

  • Exposure to gastric acid and pepsin contributes to ulcer formation

  • Commonly associated with H. pylori infection and NSAID use

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Fundus → Rare site for gastric ulcer.

  • Greater curvature → Uncommon site; ulcers here raise suspicion for malignancy.

  • Pyloric antrum → Common site of gastritis and H. pylori colonization, but typical gastric ulcer location is along the lesser curvature.

High-yield points:

Gastric ulcer:

  • Most common site → Lesser curvature near incisura angularis

  • Duodenal ulcer → First part of duodenum (duodenal bulb)

Exam pearl:
Typical gastric ulcer site = Lesser curvature.

Anatomy-05.question: ১৮) Esophagus starts at
১৯) Outermost muscular layer of stomach
২০) Fixed part of small intestine
Anatomy-05.exp:
The correct answer is duodenum. The duodenum is the fixed part of the small intestine because most of it is retroperitoneal and firmly attached to the posterior abdominal wall.

Features:

  • C-shaped structure around the head of pancreas

  • Mostly immobile

  • Receives bile and pancreatic secretions

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Jejunum → Intraperitoneal and mobile; attached by mesentery.

  • Ileum → Intraperitoneal and mobile; attached by mesentery.

  • Ilium → A bone of the pelvis, not a part of the intestine.

High-yield points:

Small intestine:

  • Duodenum → Fixed part

  • Jejunum + ileum → Mobile parts (suspended by mesentery)

Exam pearl:
Fixed part of small intestine = Duodenum.

Anatomy-05.question: ২১) Cardinal features of large intestine except-
Anatomy-05.exp:
The correct answer is Valvulae conniventes because they are features of the small intestine, not the large intestine.

Cardinal features of large intestine:

  • Taeniae coli → Three longitudinal muscle bands

  • Sacculations (haustra) → Pouch-like dilatations

  • Appendices epiploicae → Fat-filled peritoneal tags

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Taeniae coli → Present in colon.

  • Sacculations/haustra → Present in colon.

  • Appendices epiploicae → Present in colon.

High-yield points:

Structure Location
Taeniae coli Large intestine
Haustra Large intestine
Appendices epiploicae Large intestine
Valvulae conniventes (plicae circulares) Small intestine

Exam pearl:
Valvulae conniventes = small intestine; the other three = large intestine.

Anatomy-05.question: ২২) Inlet of inguinal canal situated in-
Anatomy-05.exp:
The correct answer is fascia transversalis. The deep (internal) inguinal ring, which is the inlet of the inguinal canal, is an opening in the transversalis fascia.

Anatomy of inguinal canal:

  • Deep inguinal ring (inlet) → Opening in fascia transversalis

  • Superficial inguinal ring (outlet) → Opening in external oblique aponeurosis

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Parietal peritoneum → Forms the lining of the abdominal cavity; not the site of the inguinal ring.

  • Internal oblique muscle → Forms part of the roof and contributes to the canal walls, but does not contain the deep ring.

  • External oblique → Contains the superficial inguinal ring, not the inlet.

High-yield points:

Structure Location
Deep inguinal ring (inlet) Fascia transversalis
Superficial inguinal ring (outlet) External oblique aponeurosis

Anatomy-05.question: ২৩) Inferior venacava passes through—
Anatomy-05.exp:
The correct answer is tendinous opening. The inferior vena cava (IVC) passes through the diaphragm at the caval opening (T8 level), which is located in the central tendon of the diaphragm.

Key points:

  • IVC → T8 → Caval opening → Central tendon

  • The opening is tendinous, allowing the IVC to remain open during diaphragmatic contraction.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Muscular opening → Oesophagus passes through the muscular part of diaphragm (T10).

  • Aponeurotic opening → Not the standard description of the caval opening.

  • Osseoaponeurotic opening → A type of opening between bony and aponeurotic structures, not for IVC.

High-yield diaphragm openings:

Structure Level Type of opening
IVC T8 Tendinous (central tendon)
Oesophagus T10 Muscular
Aorta T12 Musculo-aponeurotic

Exam pearl:
IVC passes through diaphragm at T8 via the central tendon (tendinous opening).

Anatomy-05.question: ২৪) Most common position of the appendix-
Anatomy-05.exp:
The correct answer is retrocecal. The most common position of the vermiform appendix is retrocecal (retrocolic), where the appendix lies behind the caecum.

Approximate positions of appendix:

  • Retrocecal/retrocolic → ~65% (most common)

  • Pelvic → ~30%

  • Subcaecal, preileal, postileal → less common

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Pelvic → Second most common position; may cause pelvic symptoms (e.g., urinary frequency, diarrhoea).

  • Preileal → Rare position, anterior to ileum.

  • Postileal → Rare position, posterior to ileum.

High-yield points:

Appendix positions:

  1. Retrocecal (most common)

  2. Pelvic

  3. Subcaecal

  4. Preileal

  5. Postileal

Exam pearl:
Most common appendix position = Retrocecal.

Anatomy-05.question: ২৫) Sympathetic Nerve supply of appendix arise from
Anatomy-05.exp:
The correct answer is T10. The sympathetic nerve supply of the appendix arises from the T10 spinal segment through the superior mesenteric plexus.

Clinical importance:

  • Visceral pain from appendix initially travels with sympathetic fibres to T10

  • This produces referred pain around the umbilicus in early appendicitis

The other options are incorrect because:

  • T9 → Related to upper abdominal visceral afferents, but not the appendix.

  • T11 and T12 → Supply lower abdominal structures but not the main sympathetic pathway of the appendix.

High-yield points:

Appendix nerve supply:

  • Sympathetic → T10 via superior mesenteric plexus

  • Parasympathetic → Vagus nerve

Appendicitis pain:

  • Early → Periumbilical pain (T10 dermatome)

  • Later → Right iliac fossa pain (parietal peritoneum irritation)

Exam pearl:
Appendix sympathetic supply = T10.

Anatomy-05.question: ২৬) Abdominal aorta begins at the level of
Anatomy-05.exp:
The correct answer is T12. The abdominal aorta begins at the level of T12 vertebra after the thoracic aorta passes through the aortic hiatus of the diaphragm.

Important anatomical points:

  • Begins: T12 (aortic hiatus)

  • Ends: L4 (bifurcation into common iliac arteries)

The other options are incorrect because:

  • T11 → Not the level of transition from thoracic to abdominal aorta.

  • L4 → Level where the abdominal aorta terminates and divides into common iliac arteries.

  • L5 → Level where the inferior vena cava is formed.

High-yield points:

Structure Vertebral level
Abdominal aorta begins T12
Aorta bifurcation L4
IVC formation L5
Caval opening T8

Exam pearl:
Abdominal aorta = starts at T12, ends at L4.

Anatomy-05.question: ২৭) Continuation of abdominal aorta
Anatomy-05.exp:
The correct answer is common iliac artery. The abdominal aorta terminates at the level of L4 vertebra by dividing into the right and left common iliac arteries.

Anatomy:

  • Abdominal aorta begins → T12

  • Abdominal aorta ends → L4

  • Termination → Right & left common iliac arteries

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Median sacral artery → A small midline branch arising from the posterior aspect of the aorta near its bifurcation.

  • Internal iliac artery → A branch of the common iliac artery, supplying pelvic organs.

  • External iliac artery → A branch of the common iliac artery that continues as the femoral artery.

High-yield points:

Abdominal aorta → L4 → Common iliac arteries → Internal + External iliac arteries

Exam pearl:
Continuation of abdominal aorta = Common iliac artery.

Anatomy-05.question: ২৮) Structure passing through esophageal opening –
Anatomy-05.exp:
The correct answer is both vagus nerves. The oesophageal hiatus of the diaphragm is located at T10 vertebral level and transmits:

  • Oesophagus

  • Anterior vagal trunk (left vagus)

  • Posterior vagal trunk (right vagus)

  • Small oesophageal vessels and lymphatics

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Thoracic duct → Passes through the aortic hiatus (T12).

  • Right phrenic nerve → Passes through the caval opening (T8) with the inferior vena cava.

  • Left phrenic nerve → Passes through the muscular part of the diaphragm, not the oesophageal hiatus.

High-yield diaphragm openings:

Opening Level Structures
Caval opening T8 IVC, right phrenic branch
Oesophageal hiatus T10 Oesophagus + both vagal trunks
Aortic hiatus T12 Aorta, thoracic duct

Exam pearl:
Oesophageal hiatus (T10) → Both vagus nerves.

Anatomy-05.question: ২৯) Gastric glands lies in-
Anatomy-05.exp:
The correct answer is lamina propria. Gastric glands are located within the lamina propria of the gastric mucosa and open into the gastric pits.

Layers of the stomach wall (inside → outside):

  1. Mucosa

    • Epithelium

    • Lamina propria (contains gastric glands)

    • Muscularis mucosae

  2. Submucosa

  3. Muscularis propria

  4. Serosa

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Muscularis propria → Contains smooth muscle layers responsible for gastric movements.

  • Submucosa → Contains blood vessels, lymphatics, and nerves, but not gastric glands.

  • Muscularis mucosa → Thin muscle layer separating mucosa from submucosa.

High-yield points:

Gastric glands:

  • Location → Lamina propria of gastric mucosa

  • Open into → Gastric pits

  • Contain:

    • Parietal cells → HCl, intrinsic factor

    • Chief cells → Pepsinogen

    • G cells → Gastrin

Exam pearl:
Gastric glands = Lamina propria of mucosa.

Anatomy-05.question: ৩০) Main artery of stomach
Anatomy-05.exp:
The correct answer is left gastric artery. It is considered the main artery of the stomach and is the smallest branch of the coeliac trunk.

Supply:

  • Runs along the lesser curvature

  • Supplies the upper part of the stomach

  • Anastomoses with the right gastric artery

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Right gastric artery → Supplies the lower part of the lesser curvature; usually a branch of the hepatic artery.

  • Left gastro-epiploic (gastro-omental) artery → Supplies the greater curvature; branch of splenic artery.

  • Splenic artery → Gives gastric branches (short gastric and left gastro-epiploic), but is not the main gastric artery.

High-yield points:

Arterial supply of stomach (coeliac trunk branches):

  • Left gastric → main artery of stomach

  • Right gastric → lesser curvature

  • Left gastro-omental → greater curvature

  • Short gastric → fundus

Exam pearl:
Main artery of stomach = Left gastric artery.

Anatomy-05.question: ৩১) Most dilated part of GIT—
Anatomy-05.exp:
The correct answer is stomach. The stomach is the most dilated part of the gastrointestinal tract (GIT) and acts as a reservoir for food.

Functions of stomach:

  • Temporary storage of food

  • Mechanical mixing

  • Initiates protein digestion

  • Regulates gastric emptying into the duodenum

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Rectum → A dilated part of the large intestine that stores faeces, but not the most dilated part of the GIT.

  • Sigmoid colon → A curved segment of the colon, not the widest part.

  • Anus → Terminal opening of GIT, not a dilated segment.

High-yield points:

Most dilated part of GIT = Stomach

Exam pearl:
Stomach is the largest dilated reservoir of the alimentary canal.

Anatomy-05.question: ৩২) Appendicular artery is a branch of
Anatomy-05.exp:
The correct answer is ileocolic artery. The appendicular artery is usually a branch of the posterior caecal artery, which arises from the ileocolic branch of the superior mesenteric artery.

Key points:

  • Appendicular artery → Ileocolic artery → Superior mesenteric artery

  • It runs within the mesoappendix to supply the appendix.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Right colic artery → Supplies ascending colon.

  • Middle colic artery → Supplies transverse colon.

  • Left colic artery → Supplies descending colon.

High-yield points:

Superior mesenteric artery branches:

  • Middle colic → Transverse colon

  • Right colic → Ascending colon

  • Ileocolic → Caecum, terminal ileum, appendix

Exam pearl:
Appendicular artery = branch of ileocolic artery.

Anatomy-05.question: ৩৩) Hirschsprung disease usually occur in—
Anatomy-05.exp:
The correct answer is sigmoid colon. Hirschsprung disease is a congenital disorder caused by the absence of ganglion cells in the myenteric (Auerbach) and submucosal (Meissner) plexuses, leading to failure of relaxation and functional obstruction.

The rectosigmoid region is the most commonly affected site.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Appendix → Not a typical site.

  • Descending colon → May be involved in longer-segment disease but less common.

  • Transverse colon → Rare involvement.

High-yield points:

Hirschsprung disease:

  • Most common site → Rectosigmoid colon

  • Pathology → Absence of enteric ganglion cells

  • Result → Distal bowel fails to relax → proximal dilatation (megacolon)

Exam pearl:
Hirschsprung disease most commonly affects rectosigmoid colon.

Anatomy-05.question: ৩৪) Which vein drain into portal system—
Anatomy-05.exp:
The correct answer is superior rectal vein. It drains into the portal venous system through:

Superior rectal vein → Inferior mesenteric vein → Splenic vein → Portal vein

The other rectal veins belong to the systemic venous circulation:

  • Middle rectal vein → Internal iliac vein → Inferior vena cava (systemic circulation)

  • Inferior rectal vein → Internal pudendal vein → Internal iliac vein → Inferior vena cava

High-yield points:

Portosystemic anastomosis at rectum:

  • Portal side: Superior rectal vein

  • Systemic side: Middle + inferior rectal veins

Clinical importance:

  • Portal hypertension → Dilated rectal veins → Anorectal varices

Exam pearl:
Superior rectal vein drains into portal system; middle and inferior rectal veins drain into systemic circulation.

Anatomy-05.question: ৩৫) Anus below the pectinate develops from—
Anatomy-05.exp:
The correct answer is proctodeum. The anus below the pectinate line develops from the proctodeum, which is an ectodermal invagination.

Embryological origin of anal canal:

Part of anal canal Origin
Above pectinate line Endoderm (hindgut)
Below pectinate line Ectoderm (proctodeum)

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Stomodium (stomodeum) → Gives rise to the oral cavity.

  • Urogenital sinus → Gives rise to parts of urinary tract and lower genital tract.

  • Urorectal sinus → Related to separation of cloaca into urogenital sinus and anorectal canal.

High-yield points:

Pectinate line significance:

  • Above → Endoderm, visceral sensation, portal drainage

  • Below → Ectoderm (proctodeum), somatic sensation, systemic drainage

Exam pearl:
Anus below pectinate line = Proctodeum (ectodermal origin).

Anatomy-05.question: ৩৬) Most dependent part of abdomen in lying position -
Anatomy-05.exp:
The correct answer is hepato-renal pouch (Morison’s pouch). In a supine (lying) position, the most dependent part of the peritoneal cavity is the hepato-renal recess, located between:

  • Right lobe of liver

  • Right kidney

Fluid such as blood, pus, or ascites tends to collect here in a supine patient.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Pelvic cavity → The most dependent part in an upright standing position (especially rectouterine/rectovesical pouch).

  • Iliac fossa → Not the lowest point of the peritoneal cavity in the supine position.

  • Greater sac → A large peritoneal compartment but not the most dependent area.

High-yield points:

Peritoneal fluid collection:

  • Supine position → Hepato-renal pouch (Morison’s pouch)

  • Upright position → Pelvic cavity (rectouterine/rectovesical pouch)

Exam pearl:
Most dependent part of abdomen in lying position = Hepato-renal pouch.

Anatomy-05.question: ৩৭) True ligament of liver—
Anatomy-05.exp:
The correct answer is falciform ligament. The true ligaments of the liver are formed by peritoneal folds that attach the liver to surrounding structures.

True ligaments of liver:

  • Falciform ligament

  • Coronary ligament

  • Right and left triangular ligaments

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Coronary ligament → Also a true ligament of the liver (so the question is slightly ambiguous), but the commonly asked single best answer is falciform ligament.

  • Ligamentum venosum → A fibrous remnant of the ductus venosus, not a true peritoneal ligament.

  • Lesser omentum → A peritoneal fold connecting liver to stomach and duodenum, not classified as a true ligament of the liver.

High-yield points:

True ligaments of liver (peritoneal folds):

  • Falciform ligament

  • Coronary ligament

  • Triangular ligaments

False ligaments (fibrous remnants):

  • Ligamentum teres (obliterated umbilical vein)

  • Ligamentum venosum (obliterated ductus venosus)

Exam pearl:
Falciform ligament = true ligament of liver.

Anatomy-05.question: ৩৮) Metabolic unit of liver
Anatomy-05.exp:
The correct answer is hepatic acini. The hepatic acinus (Rappaport acinus) is considered the functional and metabolic unit of the liver because it reflects the metabolic activity of hepatocytes according to their blood supply and oxygen gradient.

The hepatic acinus is divided into zones:

  • Zone 1 (periportal) → Highest oxygen and nutrient supply; most metabolically active

  • Zone 2 → Intermediate

  • Zone 3 (centrilobular) → Lowest oxygen; vulnerable to ischaemia and toxins

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Portal lobule → Emphasizes the exocrine function (bile secretion) of the liver.

  • Hepatic lobule → Structural/anatomical unit of the liver.

  • Hepatocyte → Functional cell of the liver, but not considered the metabolic unit.

High-yield points:

Liver unit Main significance
Classical hepatic lobule Structural unit
Portal lobule Bile secretion (exocrine function)
Hepatic acinus Metabolic/functional unit

Exam pearl:
Metabolic unit of liver = Hepatic acinus.

Anatomy-05.question: ৩৯) Alkaline fluid containing mucin is secreted from which cell of stomach?

৪১) Serous acini

Anatomy-05.option3: Thin limb of loop of Henle

Anatomy-05.question: ৪৫) Which one produces sperm?
৪৬) Red & white pulp are present in
৪৭) Normal position of uterus is:
Anatomy-05.exp:
The correct answer is anteverted and anteflexed. The normal position of the uterus is:

  • Anteversion → Uterus is tilted forward relative to the vagina.

  • Anteflexion → Body of uterus is bent forward over the cervix.

This position helps keep the uterus supported within the pelvis.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Retroverted and retroflexed → Abnormal backward tilting and bending of the uterus.

  • Anteverted and retroflexed → Mixed position; not the normal anatomical position.

  • Retroverted and anteflexed → Not the normal position.

High-yield points:

Normal uterus position:

  • Anteverted

  • Anteflexed

Exam pearl:
Normal uterus = AVAF (Anteverted + Anteflexed).

Anatomy-05.question: ৪৮) Aortic opening of diaphragm at the level of-
Anatomy-05.exp:
The correct answer is T12. The aortic opening (aortic hiatus) of the diaphragm is located at the level of the 12th thoracic vertebra.

Structures passing through the aortic hiatus:

  • Aorta

  • Thoracic duct

  • Azygos vein

The other options are incorrect because:

  • T6 → Not a diaphragm opening level.

  • T8 → Caval opening (IVC passes through central tendon).

  • T10 → Oesophageal hiatus (oesophagus + both vagal trunks).

High-yield diaphragm openings:

Opening Vertebral level Structures
Caval opening T8 IVC
Oesophageal hiatus T10 Oesophagus + vagus nerves
Aortic hiatus T12 Aorta + thoracic duct

Exam pearl:
Aortic hiatus = T12.

Anatomy-05.question: ৪৯) Accessory pancreatic duct is also called
Anatomy-05.exp:
The correct answer is Santorini duct. The accessory pancreatic duct is also known as the duct of Santorini.

Pancreatic ducts:

  • Main pancreatic duct (Wirsung duct) → Drains most of the pancreas; opens into the major duodenal papilla with the common bile duct.

  • Accessory pancreatic duct (Santorini duct) → Drains the superior part of the head of pancreas; opens into the minor duodenal papilla.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Wirsung duct → Main pancreatic duct, not accessory duct.

  • Henson's duct → Not a pancreatic duct.

  • Hoffman's duct → Not a pancreatic duct.

High-yield points:

Pancreatic ducts:

  • Main duct = Wirsung

  • Accessory duct = Santorini

Exam pearl:
Accessory pancreatic duct = Santorini duct.

Anatomy-05.question: ৫০) Blood supply of liver is
Anatomy-05.exp:
The correct answer is 80% venous, 20% arterial. The liver has a dual blood supply:

  • Portal vein → ~75–80% of blood supply

    • Carries nutrient-rich blood from the gastrointestinal tract and spleen

  • Hepatic artery → ~20–25% of blood supply

    • Supplies oxygen-rich arterial blood

Although the hepatic artery provides less blood volume, it supplies about 50% of the liver’s oxygen requirement.

The other options are incorrect because they reverse or overestimate arterial contribution.

High-yield points:

Liver blood supply:

  • Portal vein: 80% blood flow, 50% oxygen

  • Hepatic artery: 20% blood flow, 50% oxygen

Exam pearl:
Liver receives 80% venous (portal) and 20% arterial (hepatic artery) blood.
